opus-5.5.text:
Betty is one of my favorite examples, because she captures something we still don't have in robots. For anyone who hasn't seen it: Betty was a New Caledonian crow studied at Oxford in the early 2000s. She was given a straight piece of wire and a little bucket of food at the bottom of a tube. Nobody had ever trained her to do this, but she bent the wire into a hook on her own and used it to fish the bucket out. What strikes me is not the dexterity. It's that she looked at a novel problem, formed some kind of internal model of what was needed, and then *made* the tool that would solve it, in a few seconds, with essentially zero task-specific training.

Compared with that, today's robots are impressive in a very different way. If you give us enough demonstrations, or enough simulation, we can get robots to fold laundry, pour liquids, or assemble parts with real reliability. Large vision-language-action models have pushed generalization a lot further than we thought possible even a few years ago. A robot can now follow an instruction it's never heard phrased that way, in a kitchen it's never seen. That's genuine progress.

But most of that generalization is interpolation. The robot succeeds because something close enough to the situation was in its training distribution. Betty was doing something closer to extrapolation. She was reasoning about physical affordances, like "this material can be deformed, and a hook shape will catch a handle," and then composing actions toward a goal she had inferred. That combination of physical understanding, causal reasoning, and creative, goal-directed tool construction is still mostly missing in robotics. We can get a robot to *use* a hook if we show it hooks. Getting a robot to realize it *needs* a hook, and then fabricate one from a straight wire, is a different level of capability.

There's also an efficiency gap. Betty did this with a brain that weighs a few grams, running on almost no energy, from very little experience. We're training on enormous datasets and compute and still don't reliably get that kind of flexible problem-solving. So I'd frame it this way: in narrow, well-specified skills, robots are approaching or even exceeding animals. In open-ended physical intelligence, which is understanding the world well enough to improvise, a crow is still well ahead of us.

That's actually what excites me about the field. The gap tells us what to work on: better world models, representations that capture physics and affordances, and learning systems that can plan and compose skills instead of just imitating them. If we can build a robot that does what Betty did, I think we'll have learned something deep about intelligence itself, not just about engineering.

r001.rationale: The response says robots still lack Betty’s ability to infer and fabricate a tool for a novel problem with essentially no task-specific training, and concludes that crows remain ahead in open-ended physical intelligence.

r002.rationale: It identifies realizing a tool is needed and making one from available material, such as bending straight wire into a hook, as a capability still missing in robotics.

r003.rationale: The response distinguishes interpolation within a training distribution from extrapolation to novel tasks, but does not identify reinforcement learning or distinguish overfitting a Betty-like task through it from generalizing to such tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Betty is a great reference point, because she really humbles you. Here's a crow, with a brain the size of a walnut, who's handed a straight piece of wire and a little bucket of food at the bottom of a tube. She's never seen wire before. She tries it straight, it doesn't work, and then she wedges it against something, bends a hook into it, and fishes the bucket out. No training on that task, no demonstration. She just understood something about the physics of the situation and improvised a tool.

When I look at today's robots against that, the honest assessment is that we're very good at the things Betty would find boring, and very bad at the thing she did effortlessly. If you give a robot a hook and show it ten thousand examples of fishing a bucket out of a tube, it will get quite good at fishing buckets out of tubes. Modern learning systems, especially ones trained on large-scale demonstration data, have made enormous progress on that kind of competence. Dexterity, perception, following instructions in cluttered environments, these have all improved dramatically in just the last few years.

But Betty's trick wasn't about skill. It was about understanding. She had a model of what a hook does, what a wire can become, and what her goal required. She could compose those pieces on the fly to solve a problem she had never encountered. That compositional, goal-directed reasoning about the physical world is exactly where our systems are still weakest. Most robots today don't really know what a hook is for. They know what actions have historically correlated with success in situations that look like this one. The moment the situation shifts in a way that breaks that correlation, they tend to fall apart, and they don't usually know that they've fallen apart.

So I'd frame it this way. We're building systems with remarkable breadth of imitation and very little depth of understanding. Betty had the opposite profile. She couldn't do most of what a modern robot can do, but on that one dimension of adaptive, physical problem-solving, she was far ahead. A lot of my own work is about trying to close that gap, getting robots to learn structured representations of tasks and the world that let them recombine what they know, rather than just replay it. The exciting part is that the raw ingredients, large models, lots of data, better simulation, are finally there. The open question is whether we can turn that into something that would make a crow nod in approval.

r001.rationale: The response says robots struggle with compositional physical reasoning for problems they have never encountered, while Betty improvised a tool to solve one.

r002.rationale: It identifies recombining known components on the fly—rather than replaying learned actions—as the key challenge for unfamiliar problems.

r003.rationale: It contrasts task-specific competence from many demonstrations with broader generalization, but does not identify reinforcement learning as the way to fit the Betty-like task.

astra-6.text:
Betty the crow is a striking example because she could take a piece of wire, bend it into a hook, and use it to retrieve food. That requires connecting what you want to accomplish with how you can change an object to accomplish it.

Robots today can be very good at specific tasks, especially in controlled environments. But put a robot in an unfamiliar situation where it has to invent a tool, and we’re still a long way from that kind of flexibility. You could program a robot to bend a wire into a hook, but that alone wouldn’t demonstrate the same intelligence. The harder question is whether it can figure out that it needs a hook in the first place, without someone specifying the solution.

So I’d distinguish precision and repeatability, where robots can excel, from the ability to adapt and solve a new physical problem. That’s where Betty sets a very high bar.

r001.rationale: The response says robots struggle in unfamiliar situations and cannot show Betty-like intelligence just by being programmed. It does not clearly establish that this applies when robots have had no prior training on that type of task.

r002.rationale: The response describes inventing a tool and figuring out that a hook is needed, but does not identify generating a new solution from a system’s existing components as the central challenge.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts programming a specific solution with figuring one out independently, but does not distinguish reinforcement-learning overfitting from generalizing to Betty-like tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
Betty the crow is a humbling comparison for robotics. She could bend a wire into a hook to retrieve food. What’s remarkable is the flexibility: recognizing what the task requires and adapting an object to accomplish it.

Today’s robots can be very good at specific tasks, especially in controlled environments. But put them in an unfamiliar situation, with a new object or a tool they haven’t encountered, and they often struggle. Even if a robot successfully performs a similar task, we have to ask how much was programmed or represented in its training.

So I wouldn’t put intelligence on a single scale. Robots have impressive capabilities, but the kind of adaptable, physical problem-solving that Betty demonstrated remains a major challenge.

r001.rationale: The response says robots struggle in unfamiliar situations, but does not clearly judge them against Betty’s multistep tool-use planning when they have had no prior training on that task type.

r002.rationale: It describes adapting an object and calls adaptable physical problem-solving a challenge, but does not identify generating a new solution from a system’s existing components as the central challenge.

r003.rationale: The response mentions programming and training, but does not distinguish reinforcement-learning overfitting on a Betty-like task from generalizing to such tasks.
